historical_claims.anchor: Ursula K. Le Guin was born in Berkeley in 1929.
Her father, Alfred L. Kroeber, was an anthropologist; her mother, Theodora Kroeber, was a writer and biographer.
In an interview later in her career, Le Guin described The Left Hand of Darkness as a way to investigate questions about gender that were pressing on her and on the culture around her

description: Reads Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Left Hand of Darkness through Genly Ai and Estraven’s changing relationship on Gethen, the politics of Karhide and Orgoreyn and their journey across the ice. Examines the novel’s invented reproductive biology, gendered language, cross-cultural misunderstanding, exile, coercion and trust; its myths, reports and diaries; and Le Guin’s later reconsideration of her choices.
